items.title: The AI Safety Debate Has Lost the Plot. We Asked 10 Experts What the Real Nightmares Are | WIRED
items.summary: If AI is going to be one of the most significant advances in human civilization, then we should have an equally advanced political response. We should be making giant, no-regrets moves that give people and families economic resilience to withstand the changes. That is something that the richest nation on Earth at the richest moment in history, on the precipice of the greatest technological shift, can absolutely do. [...] I just think the issues presented by AI are so monstrously large, like: What is a person? What is writing? What is friendship? Would it be better to have artificial life forms than organic life forms? These are the monster questions that are typically the domain of the liberal arts, philosophy, and theology. items.title: SHE NEEDS A FAN TO STAY COOL. THAT'S THE MOST REALISTIC PART OF THIS VIDEO. 🤖🌀
items.summary:
SHE NEEDS A FAN TO STAY COOL. THAT'S THE MOST REALISTIC PART OF THIS VIDEO. 🤖🌀

a robot expo. a crowd of phones. 
a girl with a glowing metal core where her waist should be. ✨
someone holds a little fan to it. she smiles, fixes her hair. 

the face? almost certainly AI. 
the fan? that's real robotics. 🔥
every motor, every battery, every AI chip makes heat. 🌡️
heat is one of the reasons real humanoids still work in short shifts and spend hours on chargers. 

so how far have robots actually come? 👇

📅 2015: at the DARPA challenge, robots fell over opening doors.
🤸 2025: humanoids do flips, box, and dance at expos.
📦 2025: Unitree shipped 5,500+ humanoids. AgiBot's CEO said 5,000+.
🇺🇸 Tesla, Figure and Agility: about 150 each (Omdia).
🏭 Hyundai plans a factory for 30,000 robots a year by 2028.

💰 Morgan Stanley: a $5 trillion humanoid market by 2050.
ten years from falling over to doing backflips. 
but the robots that exist are still grey, bulky and plugged in. 🔌

the "robot girl" is what the hype looks like.
the fan is what the engineering looks like. 🛠️
when the real ones catch up with this video, will you be able to tell the difference? 👀

items.title: SHE WALKS LIKE A HUMAN. THEN YOU NOTICE WHAT'S MISSING.
items.summary:
SHE WALKS LIKE A HUMAN. THEN YOU NOTICE WHAT'S MISSING.

At a tech expo, a humanoid robot walks alongside a man through a crowded exhibition hall.

She's wearing a purple shirt and black shorts.

Her movements look surprisingly natural. She turns toward him, makes eye contact, and appears to respond as they interact.

People surrounding them immediately pull out their phones.

Some smile. Others lean forward to get a better look.

But there's something unusual about her appearance.

Her entire midsection is exposed, revealing metal components, mechanical joints, cables, and illuminated electronics.

Yet she moves with the confidence and body language of a person walking through a crowd.

The interesting part isn't just how human-like she looks.

It's how naturally she fits into an ordinary social interaction.

Humanoid robots are moving beyond factory demonstrations.

And the companies that make them feel comfortable around people could be entering a much bigger market than anyone expected.

items.title: FROM THE SHOULDERS UP SHE PASSES FOR HUMAN. THEN YOU LOOK AT HER WAIST.
items.summary:
FROM THE SHOULDERS UP SHE PASSES FOR HUMAN. THEN YOU LOOK AT HER WAIST.

A humanoid robot at a tech expo, standing next to her engineer. Lilac crop top, long dark hair, a face you would walk past on the street without a second look.

He tells her she did great. She smiles, tilts her head and holds his eyes like anyone taking a compliment.

Now look below the top. There is no stomach. Just blue light, wires and a mechanical core where a waist should be. When he puts a hand on her shoulder, the core glows warm orange.

That is the part that gets people. Not the machinery. The timing. The smile lands at the right moment and for a second you forget what you are looking at.

Robots used to be judged on how well they walk. These ones are judged on how human they feel standing next to you.

Would you notice before you saw the waist?

items.title: SHE LOOKS HUMAN. EVEN HER REACTIONS ARE STARTING TO FEEL REAL.
items.summary:
SHE LOOKS HUMAN. EVEN HER REACTIONS ARE STARTING TO FEEL REAL.

At a tech expo, a young woman approaches a humanoid robot and says, “I love your hair.”

The robot smiles, touches its hair, and responds to her.

People nearby stop to watch. Some pull out their phones. Others step closer to see how it reacts.

But look beneath its face.

Exposed wires, motors, and glowing electronic components reveal the machinery behind the human appearance.

The interesting part is how quickly humanoid robots are moving beyond basic movement and industrial tasks. They're now being designed to look human, express emotions, and interact naturally with people.

The technology still has a long way to go. But once robots combine realistic faces, natural movement, and convincing conversation, the potential market could be much bigger than people expect.

Some companies may end up selling more than robots.

They may be selling the feeling of interacting with another human.

someone holds a little fan to it. she smiles, fixes her hair. 

the face? almost certainly AI. 
the fan? that's real robotics. 🔥
every motor, every battery, every AI chip makes heat. 🌡️
heat is one of the reasons real humanoids still work in short shifts and spend hours on chargers. 

so how far have robots actually come? 👇

📅 2015: at the DARPA challenge, robots fell over opening doors.
🤸 2025: humanoids do flips, box, and dance at expos.
📦 2025: Unitree shipped 5,500+ humanoids. AgiBot's CEO said 5,000+.
🇺🇸 Tesla, Figure and Agility: about 150 each (Omdia).
🏭 Hyundai plans a factory for 30,000 robots a year by 2028.

💰 Morgan Stanley: a $5 trillion humanoid market by 2050.
ten years from falling over to doing backflips. 
but the robots that exist are still grey, bulky and plugged in. 🔌

the "robot girl" is what the hype looks like.
the fan is what the engineering looks like. 🛠️
when the real ones catch up with this video, will you be able to tell the difference? 👀

items.title: SHE WALKS LIKE A HUMAN. THEN YOU NOTICE WHAT'S MISSING.
items.summary:
SHE WALKS LIKE A HUMAN. THEN YOU NOTICE WHAT'S MISSING.

At a tech expo, a humanoid robot walks alongside a man through a crowded exhibition hall.

She's wearing a purple shirt and black shorts.

Her movements look surprisingly natural. She turns toward him, makes eye contact, and appears to respond as they interact.

People surrounding them immediately pull out their phones.

Some smile. Others lean forward to get a better look.

But there's something unusual about her appearance.

Her entire midsection is exposed, revealing metal components, mechanical joints, cables, and illuminated electronics.

Yet she moves with the confidence and body language of a person walking through a crowd.

The interesting part isn't just how human-like she looks.

It's how naturally she fits into an ordinary social interaction.

Humanoid robots are moving beyond factory demonstrations.

And the companies that make them feel comfortable around people could be entering a much bigger market than anyone expected.

items.title: FROM THE SHOULDERS UP SHE PASSES FOR HUMAN. THEN YOU LOOK AT HER WAIST.
items.summary:
FROM THE SHOULDERS UP SHE PASSES FOR HUMAN. THEN YOU LOOK AT HER WAIST.

A humanoid robot at a tech expo, standing next to her engineer. Lilac crop top, long dark hair, a face you would walk past on the street without a second look.

He tells her she did great. She smiles, tilts her head and holds his eyes like anyone taking a compliment.

Now look below the top. There is no stomach. Just blue light, wires and a mechanical core where a waist should be. When he puts a hand on her shoulder, the core glows warm orange.

That is the part that gets people. Not the machinery. The timing. The smile lands at the right moment and for a second you forget what you are looking at.

Robots used to be judged on how well they walk. These ones are judged on how human they feel standing next to you.

Would you notice before you saw the waist?

items.title: SHE LOOKS HUMAN. EVEN HER REACTIONS ARE STARTING TO FEEL REAL.
items.summary:
SHE LOOKS HUMAN. EVEN HER REACTIONS ARE STARTING TO FEEL REAL.

At a tech expo, a young woman approaches a humanoid robot and says, “I love your hair.”

The robot smiles, touches its hair, and responds to her.

People nearby stop to watch. Some pull out their phones. Others step closer to see how it reacts.

But look beneath its face.

Exposed wires, motors, and glowing electronic components reveal the machinery behind the human appearance.

The interesting part is how quickly humanoid robots are moving beyond basic movement and industrial tasks. They're now being designed to look human, express emotions, and interact naturally with people.

The technology still has a long way to go. But once robots combine realistic faces, natural movement, and convincing conversation, the potential market could be much bigger than people expect.

Some companies may end up selling more than robots.

They may be selling the feeling of interacting with another human.

items.title: A man at a tech expo tests the touch sensors on a highly realistic humanoid, with the platform responding to pressure on
items.summary:
A man at a tech expo tests the touch sensors on a highly realistic humanoid, with the platform responding to pressure on its lips and describing what it detects.

Realistic skin, sensors, and short scripted exchanges are improving quickly. The harder part is still turning that into reliable, unsupervised work over longer periods without an operator nearby.

Appearance and basic interaction can look convincing in a short clip. Sustained autonomous tasks remain the bigger test.
